title: Biggest Lottery Winners: What Really Happened After
description: They matched the numbers, claimed the jackpot — then real life began. The untold stories of America's biggest lottery winners.
content:
The Day Everything Changed

Mavis Wanczyk was at work when she found out. The 53-year-old hospital worker from Chicopee, Massachusetts had spent more than three decades on the job at Mercy Medical Center — the kind of career that becomes its own quiet identity. On August 23, 2017, she checked her numbers and realized she had just won the $758.7 million Powerball jackpot, the largest single-ticket jackpot in U.S. history at the time. Her first call wasn't to a lawyer. It wasn't to a financial advisor. She called her boss and quit on the spot. That detail — impulsive, human, entirely understandable — tells you something the dollar figure alone never could.

That moment is the entry point into a larger truth: the biggest lottery winners in American history are defined not just by what they won, but by what they did in the minutes, months, and years that followed. The money arrived. Then the real story began.

Who Were These People Before the Win

Ordinary Lives, Extraordinary Outcomes

Mavis Wanczyk was a medical center worker who had bought her ticket at a Pride gas station. She had been playing the same numbers for years — birthdays, mostly, the kind of numbers that carry meaning before they carry money. Gloria MacKenzie, who claimed a $590.5 million Powerball jackpot in May 2013 in Florida, was 84 years old and largely unknown to her neighbors. She had allowed a fellow shopper to cut ahead of her in line at the Publix where she purchased the winning ticket — a small act of courtesy that, by some accounts, changed which ticket she ultimately chose.

Manuel Franco was 24 years old and living in Wisconsin when he won a $768.4 million Powerball jackpot in March 2019. He was young enough that the win redefined the entire trajectory of his adult life before it had really started. Edwin Castro, who claimed the record $2.04 billion Powerball jackpot on November 8, 2022, in California, was similarly young and private — a man whose life before the win was largely undocumented by design, and whose life after it became the subject of intense public curiosity.

Then there were Merle and Patricia Butler of Red Bud, Illinois — a retired couple who, in March 2012, shared in one of three winning tickets for the $656 million Mega Millions jackpot. They waited months before coming forward, retaining legal counsel and taking deliberate steps before facing the public. Their patience was itself a kind of wisdom.

The Claim — Chaos, Lawyers, and Anonymity Attempts

The Hours Between Winning and Telling the World

Claiming a jackpot of this magnitude is not a simple errand. Winners typically have between 90 days and a year to come forward, depending on the state, and many use that window strategically. The Butlers waited months. Castro's claim, filed in California, was processed quietly. Wanczyk came forward within days — holding a press conference that made her an overnight national figure and, by her own account, overwhelmed her completely.

The legal machinery that surrounds these claims is significant. Most attorneys advise winners to establish a trust before claiming, keeping the winner's name off public records wherever state law allows. California lottery rules require public disclosure of winners' names, which is why Castro's identity eventually became known. Other states offer more protection. All state lottery guides differ on anonymity provisions, and that difference matters enormously to people suddenly worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

Jack Whittaker, who won a $314.9 million Powerball jackpot in December 2002 in West Virginia — the largest jackpot won by a single ticket at that time — came forward almost immediately and publicly. He was already a successful businessman, and he believed he could handle the exposure. What followed became one of the most widely documented cautionary narratives in lottery history, involving legal disputes, personal losses, and years of turmoil that he himself later connected to the win.

The Longer Story — What the Money Actually Did

Real Decisions, Real Consequences

What do you do with a billion dollars? The honest answer, for most winners, is that you start by doing a few very human things. Wanczyk said she planned to take care of her family and finally relax — modest language for a transformative sum. Castro reportedly purchased a $25.5 million Hollywood Hills mansion within months of claiming his prize, a move documented by real estate records. The 2016 Powerball jackpot of $1.586 billion, split among three winning tickets in California, Florida, and Tennessee, meant each lump-sum winner took home roughly $327 million before federal taxes — still a staggering sum, though the gap between the advertised jackpot and the after-tax reality surprises many people. You can estimate the difference using a lottery tax calculator before you ever picture yourself in their shoes.

The documented choices winners make tend to cluster into recognizable categories:

  • Immediate family support — paying off mortgages, covering medical bills, funding children's education
  • Real estate purchases, often substantial
  • Legal and financial structures: trusts, advisors, estate planning
  • Charitable giving, though the scope varies widely and is often not publicly disclosed
  • Career exits — sometimes immediate, as with Wanczyk, sometimes gradual

What's less often reported is what winners describe as the social cost: the relatives they hadn't heard from in years, the friends who changed, the strangers who sent letters. Whittaker, in multiple interviews over the years, described the experience of sudden extreme wealth as isolating in ways he hadn't anticipated. MacKenzie, who was 84 when she won, had the advantage of a life already largely shaped — fewer decades ahead in which the money could complicate things.

A Winner's Own Words

"I just want to be a little more relaxed. I just want to have fun. I just want to enjoy my life." — Mavis Wanczyk, at her press conference after claiming the $758.7 million Powerball jackpot, August 2017

It's worth sitting with that quote for a moment. Here was a woman who had just become one of the wealthiest private individuals in Massachusetts, speaking not about mansions or yachts or foundations, but about relaxation and fun. The scale of the money hadn't yet reshaped the vocabulary she used to describe what she wanted from life. That gap — between the number and the feeling — is where the most human part of these stories lives.

Patterns and Insights Across the Biggest Wins

What the Stories Have in Common

Across the documented histories of the biggest lottery winners, a few patterns emerge clearly. First, the winners who fared best in public accounts were those who moved slowly — who hired lawyers before claiming, established trusts, and limited their public exposure. The Butlers of Illinois exemplify this approach. Second, winners who were already financially stable before the win — like Whittaker, a successful contractor — didn't necessarily navigate the aftermath more smoothly than those who weren't. The money introduced complications that had nothing to do with financial literacy.

Third, age appears to matter in ways that aren't simply about experience. MacKenzie, at 84, had a settled life into which the money arrived. Franco, at 24, had his entire adult life ahead to define — and to be defined by the win. Castro, similarly young, has kept a deliberately low profile, which is itself a choice that reflects how differently people absorb an event of this magnitude. And finally: the taxes are always larger than people expect. The advertised jackpot is never the number that arrives in the account. That gap, for the biggest jackpots, runs into the hundreds of millions of dollars.
